media.title: Does multiplying three, four, five by any k always give a triple?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: Right triangles have sides three k, four k and five k units. Keeping k as a letter, the squares of the three sides are worked out and compared.

video_script.why: The pattern held for two, three and four, but how can you be sure it holds for every k, when you cannot test them all?

marks.k: a blank card marked k appears
marks.ask: (3k, 4k, 5k) is written into the anchor band with a question mark
marks.book: a small title card Book question appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='seen'/>Three, four, five is a triple, and so is six, eight, ten.
<bookmark mark='k'/>Take any counting number, and call it k. Three k means three times k.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is three k, four k, five k a triple for every k?
beats.on_screen: a small title card reads Book question; (3, 4, 5) and (6, 8, 10) appear with ticks; then k appears on a blank card; (3k, 4k, 5k) is written into the anchor band with a question mark

marks.stop: the words every k are underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud, and say why you think so.
beats.on_screen: the anchor question stays; the words every k are underlined in the accent colour and the frame holds

marks.row: three right triangles appear, drawn to scale
marks.letter: the sides of one triangle are relabelled 3k, 4k and 5k
marks.endless: a row of ever bigger triangles fades off to the right

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>Here are right triangles for k equal to one, two and three.
Their sides are three k, four k and five k units.
<bookmark mark='endless'/>We cannot test every k, because the counting numbers never end.
<bookmark mark='letter'/>Instead, we keep k as a letter and square each side.
beats.on_screen: right triangles for k = 1, 2 and 3 lie in a row, drawn to scale with sides 3, 4, 5 then 6, 8, 10 then 9, 12, 15 units; a long row of triangles fades off to the right with dots; then the three sides are labelled 3k, 4k and 5k

marks.five: the slip card writes 5 × k² beside 7k² and the two do not match
marks.full: 3k × 3k is written in the working band
marks.strike: the slip card is struck through in the warning colour

beats.colours: the slip = warning; k = any counting number
narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='slipsay'/>A common slip says squaring three k gives three times k squared. Four k gives four times k squared, and together that is seven k squared.
[chintu] <bookmark mark='five'/>The slip then says squaring five k gives five times k squared, so seven is not five.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>That slip squares only the k, and forgets the three, the four and the five.
<bookmark mark='full'/>The square of three k means three k times three k, both parts included.
beats.on_screen: the slip card shows (3k)² written as 3k² and (4k)² as 4k², adding to 7k², beside 5k²; it is struck through in the warning colour; the working band writes 3k × 3k

narration: <bookmark mark='nine'/>Three times three is nine, and k times k is k squared. That gives nine k squared.
<bookmark mark='sixteen'/>In the same way, the square of four k is sixteen k squared.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Add them, and nine k squared plus sixteen k squared is twenty-five k squared.
beats.on_screen: the working band shows (3k)² = 3k × 3k = 9k², then (4k)² = 4k × 4k = 16k², then 9k² + 16k² = 25k²

marks.yes: the anchor question gets a tick
marks.note: a notebook line appears with k kept on every step
marks.endless: the words infinitely many triples appear

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>The square of five k is five k times five k, which is twenty-five k squared.
<bookmark mark='match'/>Both give twenty-five k squared, whatever number k is.
<bookmark mark='yes'/>That means three k, four k, five k is a triple for every counting number k.
<bookmark mark='endless'/>Each new k gives a new triple, so the triples never run out.
<bookmark mark='note'/>In your notebook, keep k as a letter on every line.
beats.on_screen: the working band shows (5k)² = 5k × 5k = 25k²; the two 25k² light up together; the anchor gets a tick; then the words infinitely many triples appear under the anchor; a notebook line keeps k on every step

marks.way: the line keep the number as a letter appears
marks.yours: the question about k = 11 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>To show something for every number, keep the number as a letter.
<bookmark mark='yours'/>Your turn, put k equal to eleven. Which triple do you get, and does it pass the squaring test?
beats.on_screen: the stage clears except the anchor; one line appears: keep the number as a letter to prove it for every number; then the question what triple does k = 11 give, and does it pass? appears with no answer

video_script.anchor: Is (3k, 4k, 5k) a triple for every counting number k?
video_script.design: One idea: a letter stands for every number at once, so one calculation proves it for all k. Assumes: the pattern with two, three and four, and squaring a number. Wrong idea: a common slip squares only the k. Transitions: the anchor question stays all video; the triangles leave at the ground to break boundary; one clear before the recap.
source: Book question: Is (3k, 4k, 5k) a Baudhāyana triple for every positive integer k?
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip squares only the k, writing the square of three k as three k squared and the square of four k as four k squared; it gets seven k squared against five k squared and says it fails; the working band writes three k times three k in full and shows nine k squared
maths_rules: the slip: he writes (3k)^2 as 3k^2 and (4k)^2 as 4k^2, adds to 7k^2, and compares with 5k^2; both of his squares are wrong
each counting number k gives a different triple (3k, 4k, 5k), so there are infinitely many triples
right triangles in the anchor are drawn with sides of 3k, 4k and 5k units with the right angle between the 3k and 4k sides; the stage shows k = 1, 2 and 3 as examples only
video_script.payoff_line: That means three k, four k, five k is a triple for every counting number k

final_answer.value: Yes, for every k, so there are infinitely many triples
final_answer.spoken: yes, a triple for every counting number k

video_script.substitution: Keep k as a letter and square each side: nine k squared plus sixteen k squared is twenty-five k squared, whatever k is.

media.teaching_notes: The one idea is to keep k as a letter so one calculation covers every k at once. Watch for the common slip of squaring only the k: the square of three k is nine k squared, not three k squared.

interaction_points.answer: Yes, for every k, so there are infinitely many triples

media.title: Divide a triple by its common factor: is it still a triple?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: Every side of a right triangle is divided by the same number. Nine, twelve, fifteen is divided by three and tested, and then the general case is shown by writing each number as f times a smaller number and dividing both sides by f squared.

video_script.why: Scaling up keeps a triple; does scaling down, by dividing out a common factor, keep it too?

marks.ask: the general question with a, b, c and f is written into the anchor band
marks.div: a ÷ 3 arrow points to empty parentheses with a question mark
marks.book: a small title card Book question appears
marks.nine: (9, 12, 15) appears with a tick and the tag common factor 3

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Nine, twelve, fifteen is a triple, and three divides all three numbers.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Divide each number by three. Is the new set still a triple?
<bookmark mark='ask'/>And does this work for any triple and any common factor f?
beats.on_screen: a small title card reads Book question; (9, 12, 15) is written with a tick; a tag common factor 3 appears under it; a ÷ 3 arrow points to an empty pair of parentheses with a question mark; the general question with a, b, c and f is written into the anchor band

marks.stop: the empty parentheses are underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud, for nine, twelve, fifteen first.
beats.on_screen: the anchor stays; the empty parentheses are underlined in the accent colour and the frame holds

marks.fp: a = fp, b = fq, c = fr is written in the working band
marks.big: a large right triangle with sides 9, 12 and 15 appears
marks.shrink: the triangle shrinks, every side divided by the same number
marks.letters: the labels a, b, c and the common factor f appear

beats.removed: the ÷ 3 arrow from the hook (part boundary)
narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>Here is a right triangle with sides nine, twelve and fifteen units.
<bookmark mark='shrink'/>Shrink it by dividing every length by the same number.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>In letters, call the triple eigh, b, c, with a common factor f.
<bookmark mark='fp'/>Then eigh is f times p, b is f times q, and c is f times r.
beats.on_screen: a large right triangle with sides 9, 12 and 15 units shrinks, every side divided by the same number; then the working band writes a = fp, b = fq, c = fr

marks.no: 12² = 144 is written and (6, 9, 12) is struck through in the warning colour
marks.div2: the take away arrow turns into a ÷ 3 arrow

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='slipsay'/>A common slip takes three away from each number, and gets six, nine, twelve.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Six squared plus nine squared is thirty-six plus eighty-one, which is one hundred and seventeen.
<bookmark mark='no'/>Twelve squared is one hundred and forty-four, so that fails.
<bookmark mark='div2'/>That slip took three away, but we must divide by three.
beats.on_screen: the slip card shows (9, 12, 15) with a take away 3 arrow to (6, 9, 12); the working band shows 6² + 9² = 36 + 81 = 117 and 12² = 144; (6, 9, 12) is struck through in the warning colour

marks.five: 5² = 25 is written and the parentheses fill with (3, 4, 5) with a tick

narration: <bookmark mark='d'/>Nine, twelve and fifteen divided by three give three, four and five.
<bookmark mark='t'/>Three squared plus four squared is nine plus sixteen, which is twenty-five.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five squared is twenty-five, so three, four, five is a triple.
beats.on_screen: the working band shows 9 ÷ 3 = 3, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 15 ÷ 3 = 5; then 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 and 5² = 25; the empty parentheses fill with (3, 4, 5) and get a tick

marks.fsq: f²p² + f²q² = f²r² is written under it
marks.sub: fp, fq and fr slide in over a, b and c
marks.yes: the anchor question gets a tick
marks.note: the notebook layout with three steps appears
marks.divide: each f² fades out as every term is divided by f²

narration: <bookmark mark='start'/>For any triple, eigh squared plus b squared equals c squared.
<bookmark mark='sub'/>Put f p for eigh, f q for b, and f r for c.
<bookmark mark='fsq'/>Squaring each one gives f squared p squared plus f squared q squared equals f squared r squared.
<bookmark mark='divide'/>Divide every part by f squared.
<bookmark mark='left'/>We are left with p squared plus q squared equals r squared.
<bookmark mark='yes'/>That means eigh over f, b over f, c over f is always a triple.
<bookmark mark='note'/>In your notebook, write the three lines one under another, with f squared crossed out.
beats.on_screen: the working band shows a² + b² = c²; then f²p² + f²q² = f²r²; every term is divided by f², each f² fading out; p² + q² = r² is left; the anchor gets a tick; a notebook line shows the three steps one under another
beats.moves_through: fp, fq and fr slide over a, b and c; each is equal to the letter it covers, so it may

marks.way: the line divide by a common factor, never take away appears
marks.yours: the new set (35, 84, 91) appears with a question mark

narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>Dividing a triple by a common factor gives a smaller triple, but taking away never does.
<bookmark mark='yours'/>Your turn, divide thirty-five, eighty-four, ninety-one by its largest common factor. Which triple do you get?
beats.on_screen: the stage clears except the anchor; one line appears: divide by a common factor, never take away; then the new set (35, 84, 91) appears with a question mark and no answer

video_script.anchor: If (a, b, c) has a common factor f, is (a/f, b/f, c/f) a triple? Check with (9, 12, 15).
video_script.design: One idea: dividing out a common factor divides every square by f squared, so the balance stays. Assumes: common factor, and the proof that scaling up keeps a triple. Wrong idea: a common slip takes away instead of dividing. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the large triangle leaves at the ground to break boundary; one clear before the recap.
source: Book question: If (a, b, c) has a common factor f greater than 1, is (a/f, b/f, c/f)
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip takes three away from each number and gets six, nine, twelve; thirty-six plus eighty-one is one hundred and seventeen, and twelve squared is one hundred and forty-four, so it fails
maths_rules: general case: a = fp, b = fq, c = fr with p, q, r counting numbers; a^2 + b^2 = c^2 becomes f^2 p^2 + f^2 q^2 = f^2 r^2; dividing every term by f^2 (not zero) gives p^2 + q^2 = r^2; and p = a/f, q = b/f, r = c/f
the shrinking picture: a right triangle drawn with sides 9, 12, 15 units shrinks to sides 3, 4, 5 units, drawn to scale
your turn: (35, 84, 91); largest common factor 7; (35, 84, 91) ÷ 7 = (5, 12, 13); check 1225 + 7056 = 8281 = 91^2; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: eigh over f, b over f, c over f is always a triple

final_answer.value: Yes: (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple; (9, 12, 15) gives (3, 4, 5)
final_answer.spoken: yes, eigh over f, b over f, c over f is always a triple

video_script.substitution: Write each number as f times a smaller number; every square then carries f squared, and dividing it out leaves a smaller balance.

media.teaching_notes: The one idea is that dividing every number by a common factor divides every square by f squared, so the balance stays. Watch for the common slip of taking away three instead of dividing by three; six, nine, twelve is not a triple.

interaction_points.answer: Yes: (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple; (9, 12, 15) gives (3, 4, 5)
covers: Book question: If (a, b, c) has a common factor f greater than 1, is (a/f, b/f, c/f)
interaction_points.prompt: Say your answer out loud, for nine, twelve, fifteen first.

media.title: Is any scaled version of a primitive triple primitive?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: A chart has one row for each primitive triple up to twenty and columns that multiply by two, three, four, five and six. All fifteen scaled versions are filled in, and each one is checked for a common factor.

video_script.why: If you start from a primitive triple and scale it, does the new triple stay primitive?

media.title: Is five, twelve, thirteen primitive, and which others up to 20 are?
media.context: Class 8 'The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'. Worked video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea.
media.description: A triangle with sides six, eight and ten is cut into equal segments. The longest segment that fits every side shows the common factor, and the six triples up to twenty are sorted into scaled ones and primitive ones.

video_script.why: Which triples are copies of a smaller triple, and which ones are not a copy of anything?

marks.ask: (5, 12, 13) gets a question mark
marks.six: the six triples up to 20 are written into the anchor band
marks.book: a small title card Book question appears
marks.define: the card primitive triple, no common factor bigger than 1 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Six triples have all their numbers up to twenty.
<bookmark mark='define'/>A triple is called primitive when no number bigger than one divides all three of its numbers exactly.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is five, twelve, thirteen primitive? Which other triples up to twenty are primitive?
beats.on_screen: a small title card reads Book question; the six triples up to 20 are written in the anchor band; a card appears: primitive triple, no common factor bigger than 1; then (5, 12, 13) gets a question mark

marks.stop: the question mark beside (5, 12, 13) is underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud, and name the primitive ones.
beats.on_screen: the six triples stay; the question mark beside (5, 12, 13) is underlined in the accent colour and the frame holds

marks.same: equal segments of length 2 fill the three sides
marks.common: the label common factor 2 appears beside the frame
marks.triangle: an empty triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='triangle'/>Here is a triangle with sides six, eight and ten units.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Equal segments of length two fill every side exactly.
<bookmark mark='common'/>A number that divides all three numbers is called a common factor.
beats.on_screen: a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 units is laid out; equal segments of length 2 fill every side, 3, 4 and 5 segments; the label common factor 2 appears

marks.all: the slip card is struck through in the warning colour
marks.check: 5 ÷ 2 and 13 ÷ 2 are tried and each gets a cross

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='slipsay'/>A common slip says twelve is even, so two divides it. Then it says five, twelve, thirteen is not primitive.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Two divides twelve, but it does not divide five or thirteen.
<bookmark mark='all'/>A common factor must divide all three numbers, not only one.
beats.on_screen: the slip card shows 12 ÷ 2 = 6 with the word even; the working band tries 2 on each number: 5 ÷ 2 and 13 ÷ 2 leave a remainder of 1 and get crosses; the slip card is struck through in the warning colour

marks.none: 2 and 3 are tried on 5 and 13 and each gets a cross
marks.prim: (5, 12, 13) in the anchor is marked primitive
marks.rods: a 5, 12, 13 triangle fills with segments of length 1 only

narration: <bookmark mark='five'/>Five is prime, so only one and five divide it.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>Does five divide twelve? No, twelve is not in the five times table.
<bookmark mark='none'/>Only one divides five and twelve both.
<bookmark mark='prim'/>That means five, twelve, thirteen is a primitive triple.
<bookmark mark='rods'/>This triangle can only be filled with segments of length one.
beats.on_screen: the working band shows 5 and 13 as prime and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3; neither 2 nor 3 divides 5 or 13; (5, 12, 13) is marked primitive; a triangle of sides 5, 12, 13 can only be filled with segments of length 1

marks.note: a notebook line shows one triple with its factors under each number
marks.eight: the factors of 8, 15 and 17 appear under them
marks.scaled: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15) and (12, 16, 20) move aside with the tags 2, 3 and 4

narration: <bookmark mark='scaled'/>Six, eight, ten has the common factor two, and nine, twelve, fifteen has three.
Twelve, sixteen, twenty has the common factor four.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three, four, five has none, because five is prime and does not divide three or four.
<bookmark mark='eight'/>Seventeen is prime, and it divides neither eight nor fifteen.

maths_rules: squares grow by L-shaped borders: 1 unit square; 1 + 3 = 4 = 2²; 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3²; 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4²
the odd numbers in order: place 1 is 1, place 2 is 3, place 3 is 5, place 4 is 7; place 4 gives 2 x 4 - 1 = 7
the odd number in place n is 2n - 1
the L that grows a square of side n - 1 into a square of side n has n unit squares across the top and n - 1 unit squares down the side: n + (n - 1) = 2n - 1 unit squares
the first n - 1 odd numbers fill a square of side n - 1, so they add to (n - 1)²; adding the odd number in place n gives (n - 1)² + (2n - 1) = n²
algebra check: (n - 1)² = n² - 2n + 1; n² - 2n + 1 + 2n - 1 = n²
the slip's rule (n - 1)² = n² - 1 fails at n = 5: (5 - 1)² = 16, but 5² - 1 = 24; 16 is not 24
your turn: show why 11² + 23 = 12² (121 + 23 = 144; 23 = 2 x 12 - 1); the working is never shown
every unit square is drawn the same size; a square of side k is drawn k unit squares by k unit squares
video_script.payoff_line: n minus one squared, plus the odd number two n minus one, makes n squared

final_answer.spoken: the first n minus one odd numbers make the smaller square, and the odd number in place n completes the bigger square

video_script.substitution: The first n - 1 odd numbers fill a square of side n - 1, and the odd number in place n is exactly the L that turns it into a square of side n.

media.teaching_notes: The one idea: the first n minus one odd numbers fill an n minus one square, and the odd number in place n is the L that completes the n square. Watch for children who square n minus one as n squared minus one.

video_script.anchor: 25 is an odd square. Which triple does it make?
video_script.design: One idea: add one, then halve, to find the place of an odd square. Assumes the rule (n - 1)² + (2n - 1) = n² and the triple from 9. Wrong idea: a common slip halves first and drops the half. The anchor question and the square of dots stay all video; the working band clears before the idea part and before the recap.
source: Book question: 25 is an odd square. Use it to make a triple.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip halves 25 and drops the half, so n = 12; then 11² + 25 = 146 but 12² = 144, and the line is struck.
maths_rules: 25 = 5 x 5 = 5², and 25 is odd, so 25 is an odd square
place of an odd number: add 1, then halve; (25 + 1) / 2 = 26 / 2 = 13, so n = 13
25 = 5², so 12² + 5² = 13²; the triple is (5, 12, 13), written smallest first
the slip: 25 / 2 = 12.5, he drops the half and takes n = 12; (12 - 1)² + 25 = 121 + 25 = 146, but 12² = 144; 146 is not 144
the dots are drawn as a 5 by 5 square, 25 dots
video_script.payoff_line: The triple is five, twelve and thirteen

final_answer.spoken: five, twelve and thirteen

video_script.substitution: Add one and halve: 25 is the odd number in place 13, so (13 - 1)² + 25 = 13², and 25 is 5².

media.teaching_notes: The one idea: to find the place of an odd number, add one and then halve. Watch for children who halve first and drop the half, which gives n = 12 and a line that does not balance.

video_script.design: One idea: an odd square's place n gives the other two numbers of the triple. Assumes the rule (n - 1)² + (2n - 1) = n². video_script.wrong_move: A common slip takes 9 as its own place, so n = 9; then 8² + 9 = 73 but 9² = 81, and the line is struck.
maths_rules: 9 = 3 x 3 = 3², and 9 is odd, so 9 is an odd square
the odd numbers in order: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; 9 is in place 5
the rule (n - 1)² + (2n - 1) = n² with n = 5: (5 - 1)² + 9 = 5², that is 4² + 9 = 5², 16 + 9 = 25

the slip's n = 9: (9 - 1)² + 9 = 64 + 9 = 73, but 9² = 81; 73 is not 81; the odd number in place 9 is 2 x 9 - 1 = 17
the nine dots are drawn as a 3 by 3 square

video_script.substitution: 9 is the odd number in place 5, so (5 - 1)² + 9 = 5², and 9 is 3², which makes three squares.

content.text:
Right Triangles Having Integer Sidelengths
In his Śulba-Sūtra (Verse 1.13) Baudhāyana lists a number of integer triples (a, b, c) that form the sidelengths of a right-triangle and therefore satisfy a² + b² = c². These include (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13) (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (12, 35, 37), and (15, 36, 39).
For this reason, such triples (a, b, c) that form the sidelengths of a right triangle (equivalently, satisfy a² + b² = c²) are called Baudhāyana triples. They are also called Baudhāyana-Pythagoras triples, Pythagorean triples, and right-angled triangle triples.
List down all the Baudhāyana triples with numbers less than or equal to 20.
Is there an unending sequence of Baudhāyana triples?
Mathematicians have answered this question and have found a method to generate all such triples! Let us take a few steps in this direction.
We have seen that (3, 4, 5) is a Baudhāyana triple.
Is (30, 40, 50) a Baudhāyana triple?
Is (300, 400, 500) a Baudhāyana triple?
The list of Baudhāyana triples having numbers less than or equal to 20 contains the following triples: (3, 4, 5), (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (12, 16, 20).
Do you see any pattern among them?
All these triples can be obtained by multiplying each term of (3, 4, 5) by a certain positive integer.

A Baudhāyana triple is three counting numbers (a, b, c) with a² + b² = c². Each one is a right triangle with whole-number sides.
To test a triple, square the two smaller numbers, add, and compare with the square of the largest.
Searching the squares from 1 to 400 finds six triples with numbers up to 20.
Four of them are (3, 4, 5) multiplied by 1, 2, 3 and 4.

content.text:
Can we form a conjecture on Baudhāyana triples based on this observation?
Conjecture: (3k, 4k, 5k) is a Baudhāyana triple, where k is any positive integer.
Is this true?
We have to check if (3k)² + (4k)² = (5k)². We have (3k)² + (4k)² = 9k² + 16k² = 25k², which is equal to (5k)². So, (3k, 4k, 5k) is indeed a Baudhāyana triple.
This shows that there are infinitely many Baudhāyana triples.
Can we further generalise the conjecture?
If (a, b, c) is a Baudhāyana triple, then (ka, kb, kc) is also a Baudhāyana triple where k is any positive integer. Is this statement true?
This statement can be shown to be true in the same way. Since (a, b, c) is a Baudhāyana triple, we have a² + b² = c². We need to check whether (ka)² + (kb)² = (kc)². (ka)² = ka × ka = k²a², and (kb)² = kb × kb = k²b². So, (ka)² + (kb)² = k²a² + k²b². Taking out the common factor, we have (ka)² + (kb)² = k²(a² + b²). Since a² + b² = c², we have (ka)² + (kb)² = k²c² = (kc)².
Thus, (ka, kb, kc) is a Baudhāyana triple if (a, b, c) is a Baudhāyana triple. We call (ka, kb, kc) a scaled version of (a, b, c).
A Baudhāyana triple that does not have any common factor greater than 1 is called a primitive Baudhāyana triple. So, (3, 4, 5) is primitive, whereas (9, 12, 15) is not.
Is (5, 12, 13) a primitive Baudhāyana triple? What are the other primitive Baudhāyana triples with numbers less than or equal to 20?
Generate 5 scaled versions of each of these primitive triples. Are these scaled versions primitive?
If (a, b, c) is non-primitive, and the integers have f, greater than 1, as a common factor, then is (a/f, b/f, c/f) a Baudhāyana triple? Check this statement for (9, 12, 15). Justify this statement.
If we can find all the primitive triples, we can find all the Baudhāyana triples.

content.text:
If (a, b, c) has a common factor f greater than 1, is (a/f, b/f, c/f) a triple? Check with (9, 12, 15).
1. (9, 12, 15) has the common factor 3.
2. Dividing by 3 gives (3, 4, 5), and 3² + 4² = 5².
3. In general write a = fp, b = fq and c = fr; then f²p² + f²q² = f²r².
4. Divide both sides by f²: p² + q² = r².
Answer: Yes: (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple; (9, 12, 15) gives (3, 4, 5)

content.text:
Is (5, 12, 13) a primitive Baudhāyana triple? What are the other primitive triples with numbers up to 20?
1. 5 and 13 are prime and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3, so no factor greater than 1 divides all three.
2. Of the six triples up to 20, (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15) and (12, 16, 20) have the common factors 2, 3 and 4.
3. (3, 4, 5) and (8, 15, 17) have no common factor greater than 1.

content.text:
How do we generate more primitive triples?
We know the relation between the sum of consecutive odd numbers and square numbers. 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 2², 1 + 3 + 5 = 3².
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n². Let us express this algebraically.
For this, we need to know the nth odd number. What is it?
The nth odd number is 2n − 1. So, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 3) + (2n − 1) = n², where 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 3) is the sum of the first (n − 1) odd numbers.
What is the sum of the first (n − 1) odd numbers?
Thus, (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n².
Note that this equation could also have been directly obtained by expanding (n − 1)² and adding 2n − 1 to it.
If the nth odd number, 2n − 1, is also a square number, then we have a sum of two square numbers equal to another square number. We will use this idea to generate Baudhāyana triples.
1. 9 is an odd square. It is the 5th odd number (9 = 2 × 5 − 1). So, we have 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 5², 4² + 3² = 5².
Could we have obtained this triple using the equation (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n²?
Since we took the 5th odd number, the value of n is 5. Substituting n = 5 into the equation, we get (5 − 1)² + 9 = 5², 4² + 3² = 5².
2. 25 is an odd square. It is the 13th odd number (25 = 2 × 13 − 1). So, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 23 + 25 = 13², 12² + 5² = 13². We have n = 13. Substituting this value in the equation, we get (13 − 1)² + 25 = 13², 12² + 5² = 13².

content.text:
Adding the odd numbers from 1 gives the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on. Each new odd number wraps an L-shape around the square before it.
The nth odd number is 2n − 1, so the first n − 1 odd numbers add to (n − 1)², and (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n².
When the odd number 2n − 1 is itself a square, this is a square plus a square equal to a square: a triple.
Recipe: pick an odd square, solve 2n − 1 = that square for n, and the triple is the square root of the odd square, n − 1 and n.

content.text:
Why is (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n²?
1. 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 2² and 1 + 3 + 5 = 3²: the first n odd numbers add to n².
2. The nth odd number is 2n − 1.
3. The first n − 1 odd numbers add to (n − 1)².
4. Adding the nth odd number gives (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n².
Answer: (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n²

video_script.wrong_move: A common slip divides (12, 16, 20) by 2, gets (6, 8, 10), sees it is not primitive and calls the statement false; the factor 2 was shared but was not the biggest one, 4.
maths_rules: the factors shared by 12, 16 and 20 are 1, 2 and 4; the biggest is 4
the slip's step: (12, 16, 20) / 2 = (6, 8, 10); 6, 8 and 10 still share 2, so (6, 8, 10) is not primitive
(12, 16, 20) / 4 = (3, 4, 5); 9 + 16 = 25, still a triple; 3, 4 and 5 share no factor bigger than 1, so (3, 4, 5) is primitive; 4 x (3, 4, 5) = (12, 16, 20)
general: let f be the biggest factor shared by a, b and c in a triple (a, b, c); if f = 1 the triple is primitive
if f is more than 1: a² + b² = c² divided by f² gives (a/f)² + (b/f)² = (c/f)², so (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple
if a/f, b/f and c/f shared a factor g bigger than 1, then f x g would divide a, b and c and be bigger than f; that cannot be, so (a/f, b/f, c/f) is primitive
then (a, b, c) = f x (a/f, b/f, c/f): a scaled copy of a primitive triple

content.text:
Triples, Q2: Does this method yield non-primitive Baudhāyana triples? [Hint: Observe that among the triples generated, one of the smaller sidelengths is one less than the hypotenuse.]
1. Every triple from the method has the form (the root of the odd square, n − 1, n).
2. Any common factor of n − 1 and n also divides their difference, which is 1.
3. So n − 1 and n share no factor greater than 1, and neither can the whole triple.
Answer: No: every triple the method gives is primitive

Any common factor of n − 1 and n also divides their difference, which is 1.
So n − 1 and n share no factor greater than 1, and neither can the whole triple.

content.text:
Triples, Q3: Are there primitive triples that cannot be obtained through this method? If yes, give examples.
1. The method gives only triples in which the hypotenuse is 1 more than a side.
2. (8, 15, 17): 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17², no common factor, and 17 − 15 = 2, 17 − 8 = 9.
3. (20, 21, 29): 20² + 21² = 400 + 441 = 841 = 29², with gaps 9 and 8.
4. (12, 35, 37): 12² + 35² = 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37², with gaps 25 and 2.
5. In none of them is the hypotenuse 1 more than a side, so the method misses them.
Answer: Yes: for example (8, 15, 17), (20, 21, 29) and (12, 35, 37)

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q5: True or False: Every Baudhāyana triple is either a primitive triple or a scaled version of a primitive triple.
1. Take any triple (a, b, c) and let f be the greatest common factor of a, b and c.
2. If f = 1, the triple is primitive.
3. If f is more than 1, then (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple with no common factor greater than 1: a primitive triple.
4. And (a, b, c) is f times that primitive triple: a scaled version.
Answer: True
facts: end FiO5: every triple up to 100 is primitive or a scaled primitive
steps: Take any triple (a, b, c) and let f be the greatest common factor of a, b and c.
If f = 1, the triple is primitive.
If f is more than 1, then (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple with no common factor greater than 1: a primitive triple.
And (a, b, c) is f times that primitive triple: a scaled version.

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q6: Give 5 examples of rectangles whose sidelengths and diagonals are all integers.
1. The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle made by two of its sides.
2. So the two sides and the diagonal must form a Baudhāyana triple.
3. 3² + 4² = 5², 6² + 8² = 10², 5² + 12² = 13², 8² + 15² = 17², 7² + 24² = 25².
Answer: 3 by 4 (diagonal 5), 6 by 8 (10), 5 by 12 (13), 8 by 15 (17), 7 by 24 (25)

content.text:
A Long-Standing Open Problem
The study of Baudhāyana triples inspired the great French mathematician Fermat, who lived during the 17th century, to make a general statement about the sum of powers of positive integers.
We have seen that there are an infinite number of square numbers that can be written as a sum of two square numbers. This made Fermat wonder if there is a perfect cube that can be written as a sum of two perfect cubes, a fourth power that can be written as a sum of two fourth powers, and so on. In other words, he wondered if there is a solution to the equation xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ, where x, y, and z are natural numbers, and n > 2.
In the margin of a book that dealt with properties and patterns of positive integers (like that of Baudhāyana triples), Fermat wrote that amongst the unending sequence of numbers, one cannot find a single perfect cube that is a sum of two perfect cubes, a fourth power that is a sum of two fourth powers, and so on. So, the equation has no solution for powers greater than 2. In addition to stating this, Fermat wrote,
"I have found a truly marvellous proof of this statement, but the margin is too small to contain it".
No one could ever find Fermat's proof of this statement, which is called Fermat's Last Theorem.
After his death, many great mathematicians tried their hand at proving this theorem. There followed more than 300 years of failed attempts in proving it.
In 1963, a 10-year-old boy named Andrew Wiles read a book (The Last Problem by Eric Bell) about Fermat's Last Theorem and its history. Despite reading about the failures of so many great mathematicians, this young boy resolved to prove this theorem.
He eventually did prove this theorem in 1994!

content.text:
For squares there are infinitely many solutions of x² + y² = z². Fermat claimed that for cubes, fourth powers and every higher power there is not a single one.
Near misses exist: 6³ + 8³ = 216 + 512 = 728, just one less than 9³ = 729; and 9³ + 10³ = 729 + 1000 = 1729, just one more than 12³ = 1728.
Checking a thousand cases, or a million, cannot settle the question, because there are infinitely many cases. Only a proof covers them all.
Andrew Wiles read about the problem in 1963, at the age of 10, and proved it in 1994, more than 300 years after Fermat's note.

Is 6³ + 8³ a perfect cube?
1. 6³ = 216 and 8³ = 512.
2. 216 + 512 = 728.
3. 9³ = 729, which is 1 more than 728.
4. 8³ = 512 is too small and 9³ = 729 is too big, so 728 is not a cube.
Answer: No: 6³ + 8³ = 728, one less than 9³ = 729

When did Andrew Wiles prove Fermat's Last Theorem, and how many years after he first read about it?
1. He read The Last Problem in 1963, at the age of 10.
2. He proved the theorem in 1994.
3. 1994 − 1963 = 31.
Answer: In 1994, 31 years later

media.description: A cross-section of a lake shows light blue water over a brown bed. A teal vertical lotus stem extends from root 'R' on the bed through surface point 'P' to a pink lotus flower, with the segment above water labelled '1'. The underwater stem from 'R' to 'P' is labelled 'x'. An amber stem extends diagonally from 'R' to point 'T' on the water surface, where a second pink flower rests. media.teaching_notes: Point first at the right-angle mark at P, then run a finger along the side facing it, the bent stem RT: that is the hypotenuse, x + 1. Stress that the 1 unit above the water is not a side of the triangle; it only tells us the stem is x + 1 long. The triangle is upside down compared with most drawings, which is a good check that students find the right angle rather than the bottom side.

The root point R sits on the bed, right of centre. The upright stem is a straight vertical teal line from R up through the surface point P and on to a lotus flower 1 unit above the surface. The bent stem is a straight amber line from R up to the point T on the surface, 3 units to the left of P, with a second lotus flower resting on the water at T. The triangle R, P, T is filled with a very light green tint. A small reddish purple square marks the right angle at P. Length labels sit beside their segments in dark text; point letters sit just outside the vertices.

- Drawn to scale with one unit u: PR (depth, vertical) = 4u, the stem above the water from P to the upright flower = 1u, PT (along the surface) = 3u, RT (bent stem) = 5u; so RT equals PR plus the 1u above the water.
- The water surface and the lake bed are exactly horizontal and parallel; PR is exactly vertical, so the angle at P between PR and PT is an exact right angle.
- Exactly one right-angle mark: a small square at P, in the angle between PR (down) and PT (left). No other angle is marked.
- Exactly two lotus flowers: one at the top of the upright stem, 1u above P; one lying on the water surface at T.

Visible text:
- 1
- 3
- x
- x + 1
- P
- R
- T

- the right-angle mark anywhere other than at P, or a second right-angle mark
- the bent stem drawn shorter than, or equal to, the underwater part of the upright stem
- the bent stem drawn curved, or its tip above or below the water surface instead of on it

content.text:
Further Applications of the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem
The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem is one of the fundamental theorems of geometry. Let us see some of its applications.
A Problem from Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī
The following is a translation of a problem from Bhāskarāchārya's (Bhāskara II) Līlāvatī. Try to visualise what you read.
"In a lake surrounded by chakra and krauñcha birds, there is a lotus flower peeping out of the water, with the tip of its stem 1 unit above the water. On being swayed by a gentle breeze, the tip touches the water 3 units away from its original position. Quickly tell the depth of the lake."
At first glance, it seems like there is insufficient data to find the solution. But the solution exists!
Let x be the length of the stem inside the water. This is the required depth of the lake. Since the stem of the lotus is sticking 1 unit above the water, the total length of the stem is x + 1.
We can make a (very reasonable) assumption that the lotus stem is perpendicular to the surface of the water in the first position. With this assumption, we get a right triangle of sides 3, x and x + 1. As this satisfies the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem, we have 3² + x² = (x + 1)², 9 + x² = x² + 2x + 1.
Subtracting x² from both sides, we get 9 = 2x + 1. x = 4.
Thus, the depth of the lake is 4 units.

content.text:
Draw the stem twice: standing straight up, and bent over with its tip on the water 3 units away.
The straight stem meets the water surface at a right angle. Call the depth x; the whole stem is x + 1.
The bent stem is the same stem, so it still has length x + 1. It is opposite the right angle: the hypotenuse.
So 3² + x² = (x + 1)². The x² on both sides cancels, leaving 9 = 2x + 1, so x = 4.

content.text:
A lotus tip is 1 unit above the water. Swayed by the breeze, the tip touches the water 3 units from its original position. Find the depth of the lake.
1. Let the depth be x; the stem has length x + 1.
2. The upright stem is perpendicular to the water, so there is a right angle at the water surface.
3. The bent stem, of length x + 1, is the hypotenuse; the other sides are x and 3.
4. 3² + x² = (x + 1)².
5. 9 + x² = x² + 2x + 1.
6. Subtract x² from both sides: 9 = 2x + 1.
7. 2x = 8, so x = 4.
Answer: The lake is 4 units deep

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q3: Find the sidelength of a rhombus whose diagonals are of length 24 units and 70 units.
1. The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
2. They cut the rhombus into 4 congruent right triangles with sides 24 ÷ 2 = 12 and 70 ÷ 2 = 35.
3. Each side of the rhombus is the hypotenuse of one of them.
4. 12² + 35² = 144 + 1225 = 1369.
5. 37² = 1369, so the side is 37.
Answer: 37 units

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q8 (ii): Suppose the grid extends indefinitely. What are the possible integer-valued areas of squares you can create in this manner?
1. Every such square has area p² + q², where p and q are whole numbers of grid steps.
2. List the sums of two squares: 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 2, 0 + 4 = 4, 1 + 4 = 5, 4 + 4 = 8, 0 + 9 = 9, 1 + 9 = 10, 4 + 9 = 13, 0 + 16 = 16, 1 + 16 = 17, 9 + 9 = 18, 4 + 16 = 20, 9 + 16 = 25.
3. Numbers such as 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14 and 15 are not sums of two squares, so no grid square has those areas.
Answer: Exactly the counting numbers that are a sum of two squares: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25 and so on

maths_rules: a square with corners on grid dots has a side that goes p grid steps across and q grid steps up (whole numbers)
that side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs p and q, so the area of the square is p² + q²
every pair p, q gives a real grid square: from (0, 0) the corners are (p, q), (p - q, p + q) and (-q, p)
area 2: p = 1, q = 1, 1 + 1 = 2, a tilted square
area 4: p = 2, q = 0, 4 + 0 = 4, the straight 2 by 2 square
area 5: p = 1, q = 2, 1 + 4 = 5, a tilted square
area 3: any square number from 4 up is too big, so both squares are 0 or 1; the sums are 0, 1 and 2; never 3
square numbers: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25
not sums of two squares: 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15 (and 19, 21, 22, 23, 24 below 25)
check by counting, area 5: the tilted square fits in a 3 by 3 square; 9 - 4 × (1 × 2 ÷ 2) = 9 - 4 = 5

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q8 (i): Using the dots of a grid as the vertices, can you create a square that has an area of (a) 2 sq. units, (b) 3 sq. units, (c) 4 sq. units, and (d) 5 sq. units?
1. A square with its corners on grid dots has a side that goes p dots across and q dots up, so its area is p² + q².
2. (a) p = 1, q = 1: 1² + 1² = 2, a tilted square of area 2.
3. (c) p = 2, q = 0: an upright 2 by 2 square, area 4.
4. (d) p = 1, q = 2: 1² + 2² = 5, a tilted square of area 5.
5. (b) 3 is not a sum of two squares: 0 + 1, 1 + 1, 0 + 4 and 1 + 4 give 1, 2, 4 and 5, never 3.
Answer: Yes for areas 2, 4 and 5; no square of area 3 is possible

content.text:
Chapter Exercises, Q9: Find the area of an equilateral triangle with sidelength 6 units. [Hint: Show that an altitude bisects the opposite side. Use this to find the height.]
1. Drop the altitude from the top vertex to the base; it makes two right triangles.
2. They have equal hypotenuses (6), the altitude in common and right angles, so they are congruent and the altitude bisects the base into 3 and 3.
3. In one right triangle: 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27, so h² = 27 and h = √27.
4. 5.1² = 26.01 and 5.2² = 27.04, so 5.1 < √27 < 5.2.
5. Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 6 × √27, which is 3√27.
6. 3√27 = 9√3 ≈ 15.59.
Answer: 3√27 = 9√3 square units, about 15.59 square units

content.text:
SUMMARY
The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem is one of the most fundamental theorems in geometry. It expresses the relationship among the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
If a, b, c, are the sidelengths of a right-angled triangle, where c is the length of hypotenuse, then a² + b² = c².
In an isosceles triangle with sidelengths a, a, c, we have the relation a² + a² = 2a² = c², i.e., c = a√2.
The number √2 lies between 1.414 and 1.415. However, it cannot be expressed as a terminating decimal. It also cannot be expressed as a fraction m/n with m, n positive integers.
A triple (a, b, c) of positive integers satisfying a² + b² = c² is called a Baudhāyana-Pythagoras triple. Examples include (3, 4, 5), (6, 8, 10), and (5, 12, 13). Infinitely many such triples can be constructed.
The equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no solution in positive integers when n > 2. This is known as 'Fermat's Last Theorem'. It was proven by Andrew Wiles in 1994.
Find the Colours!
There are 3 closed boxes: one containing only red balls, the second containing only blue balls and the third containing only green balls. The boxes are labelled RED, BLUE and GREEN such that 'no' box has the correct label. We need to find which label goes with which box. How can this be done if we are allowed to open only one box?

content.text:
Find the Colours! Three boxes hold only red, only blue and only green balls. Every label (RED, BLUE, GREEN) is wrong. Open one box only. How do you fix the labels?
1. No label is correct, so each box has a wrong label.
2. Open the box labelled RED and take out one ball; it is blue or green, never red.
3. Say it is blue: that box is BLUE.
4. The box labelled GREEN cannot hold green (its label is wrong) and cannot hold blue (already found), so it holds red.
5. The box labelled BLUE then holds green.
6. If the ball is green instead, the box labelled RED is GREEN, the box labelled BLUE holds red and the box labelled GREEN holds blue.
Answer: Open any one box, for example the one labelled RED; the colour seen and the fact that every label is wrong fix all three labels

objectives.objective_text: Students check their own tries against a count, finding that the square with doubled side holds 4 copies of the original, and draw the square on the diagonal that Baudhāyana gives for exactly double the area.
Students draw east-west and north-south lines to split both squares into congruent triangles, explain why the diagonal square holds 4 of them against 2, and extend the pattern to 2, 4 and 8.

Students construct the square joining the midpoints of a given square, verify that it has four equal sides and four right angles, and use congruent triangles to establish that its area is exactly half of the original square.
Students rearrange triangles cut from two identical squares into one square of double area, in two different ways, and explain from triangle counts why the area stays the same while the pieces move.

objectives.objective_text: Students find the hypotenuse of isosceles right triangles with equal sides 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9 as square roots with one-decimal bounds, and find the equal sides when the hypotenuse is 10.

objectives.strand_name: A length known by its area
objectives.objective_text: Students derive c² = 2a² by comparing the square on the hypotenuse with the square made of two copies of the triangle, for any length a of the equal sides.

objectives.strand_name: A length known by its area
objectives.objective_text: Students use c² = 2a² to find the hypotenuse for equal sides 12, between 16 and 17, and the equal sides 6 for hypotenuse √72, then recheck earlier answers with the formula.

objectives.strand_name: A length known by its area
objectives.objective_text: Students find the diagonal of a square with side 5 cm as the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle, giving √50 cm with bounds, and check it with c² = 2a².
Students combine two equal squares on the diagonal, then apply Baudhāyana's rule for two different squares: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with those sides has their total area.
Students follow Baudhāyana's steps with triangles T, U, W and X, explain why the four sides are equal and every corner is x + (90 − x), and account for the areas of T, U and V.
Students cut two joined squares into three pieces, rearrange them to cover the square on the hypotenuse without gaps, state the theorem a² + b² = c², and tell why it carries two names.
Students construct squares with 3 times and 5 times the area of a given square, and a square whose area is 7² − 5², choosing the right triangle for each and checking every step.
Students measure the hypotenuse of a drawn triangle with sides 3 cm and 4 cm, about 5 cm, and confirm with 3² + 4² = 25 that it is exactly 5 cm.
Students decide whether to add or subtract squares, find a third side of 12 from hypotenuse 13 and side 5, and show that sides 5, 6 and 7 fail the rule.
Students find missing sides of right triangles in any orientation, from legs 5 cm and 12 cm to six tilted figures, and justify that the hypotenuse is always the longest side.
Students list all six Baudhāyana triples with numbers up to 20, test (30, 40, 50) and (300, 400, 500), and describe the pattern shared by the multiples of (3, 4, 5).
Students prove that (ka, kb, kc) is a triple whenever (a, b, c) is, decide which triples are primitive, and divide (9, 12, 15) by its common factor 3.
Students use (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n² with an odd square 2n − 1 to build triples, obtaining (3, 4, 5) from n = 5 and (5, 12, 13) from n = 13.

Students generate five more triples from odd squares, explain why this method gives only primitive triples, find primitive triples it misses, and give rectangles with whole-number sides and diagonals.
Students state Fermat's Last Theorem for powers above 2, test near misses such as 6³ + 8³ = 728, and retell how Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
Students search sums of two squares and of two cubes for exact hits, compare the many square hits with the cube near misses, and explain why a search alone is not a proof.
Students draw the lotus stem before and after the breeze, form 3² + x² = (x + 1)², cancel x² from both sides, and find the depth of the lake, 4 units.
Students find the side of a rhombus with diagonals 24 and 70, the possible areas of squares on a dot grid, and the height and area of an equilateral triangle with side 6.
Students match each summary statement to an example from the chapter, name what remains open, and solve the Find the Colours puzzle by opening only one box.

tool_altar_builder.doer: The student builds a square altar with exactly double the area of a given square, in any way they like: draw a square on any two pegs, or place copies and half-copies of the given altar. Each try shows its area and whether it is a square. There is no fixed path, and every try is kept.
tool_altar_builder.title: Altar Builder
tool_altar_builder.predict: Before building, tap how you plan to double the altar: double the side, put two altars together, or something else.
tool_altar_builder.invariant: The given altar never changes: its area stays 4 square units, so exactly double means 8.

tool_root_squeezer.doer: The student types a decimal and sees its square marked too small or too big against the target area, then keeps the closest pair on either side to trap the square root. Each closer pair adds one more correct digit.
tool_root_squeezer.title: Root Squeezer
tool_root_squeezer.predict: Before squaring anything, drag a pin to where you think the root sits on the number line.
tool_root_squeezer.invariant: The target area stays fixed while the bounds close in; a bigger decimal always has a bigger square.

tool_triple_hunter.doer: The student picks three numbers and tests whether a² + b² = c², scales a triple by k or divides it by a common factor, and makes new triples from odd squares. Every triple found goes on a shelf as primitive or scaled.
tool_triple_hunter.title: Triple Hunter
tool_triple_hunter.predict: Before searching, guess how many triples have all three numbers 20 or less.
tool_triple_hunter.invariant: Scaling by k multiplies every square by k², so a² + b² = c² keeps holding.

tool_halving_square.doer: Mark the midpoint of each side of a paper square and fold the four corners to the centre. Name the shape PQRS you get, then check its sides and angles, join its diagonals, match the congruent triangles and compare the areas. Use a hint when you need one, and undo any move.
tool_halving_square.title: Halving a Square
tool_halving_square.predict: After folding, name the shape PQRS before checking it: rectangle, square, triangle or something else.
tool_halving_square.invariant: The paper square never changes: PQRS is always compared with the same 8 cm square.

tool_square_doubler.doer: The student cuts paper squares along their diagonals and slides and turns the triangles to build a square of double the area, then folds a square's corners to its centre to halve it. A counter shows the triangles in each shape, so areas are compared by counting.
tool_square_doubler.title: Square Doubler
tool_square_doubler.predict: Before cutting, tap how many small triangles the doubled square will hold: 4, 6 or 8.
tool_square_doubler.invariant: The total area of the pieces stays the same when they slide, turn or fold.

tool_square_combiner.doer: The student joins two squares of sides a and b, drags a cut point along the bottom edge, makes two straight cuts and slides the two triangles into place. When the pieces close into one square with no gap, its side is the hypotenuse c and its area is a² + b².
tool_square_combiner.title: Square Combiner
tool_square_combiner.predict: Before cutting, tap where the cut point on the bottom edge should go.
tool_square_combiner.invariant: The pieces keep their areas while they slide and turn; only their positions change.

tool_power_sum_hunter.doer: The student chooses squares or cubes, moves x and y, and reads how far the sum of their powers is from the nearest perfect power. Squares hit exactly again and again; cubes only come close. A counter of cases checked keeps growing and never reaches the end.
tool_power_sum_hunter.title: Power Sum Hunter
tool_power_sum_hunter.predict: Guess: will a search up to 20 find two cubes that add up to a cube?
tool_power_sum_hunter.invariant: However far a search runs, it covers only finitely many of the infinitely many cases.

tool_isosceles_builder.doer: The student drags the equal sides of an isosceles right triangle and watches the squares on a side and on the hypotenuse: the ratio of their areas stays 2. Then they type c² and c for a given a, or a² and a for a given c.
tool_isosceles_builder.title: Isosceles Hypotenuse Builder
tool_isosceles_builder.predict: Tap yes or no: will the square on the hypotenuse stay twice the square on a side when the triangle grows?
tool_isosceles_builder.invariant: The ratio of the two square areas stays 2 as the triangle grows or shrinks.

tool_right_triangle_solver.doer: The student meets a right triangle in any orientation, taps the right angle, then the hypotenuse, chooses add or subtract, and types the missing side with its unit. Typing unlocks only after the right angle and the hypotenuse are found.
tool_right_triangle_solver.title: Right Triangle Solver
tool_right_triangle_solver.predict: For each triangle, tap the right angle and then the side you think is the hypotenuse.
tool_right_triangle_solver.invariant: Turning or flipping a triangle changes nothing: the right angle, the hypotenuse and a² + b² = c² stay the same.

tool_hidden_triangle_finder.doer: The student meets one scene at a time, a lotus in a lake, a rhombus and an equilateral triangle, taps where the right angle hides, then writes the theorem with the unknown and solves it.
tool_hidden_triangle_finder.title: Hidden Triangle Finder
tool_hidden_triangle_finder.predict: Before each scene, tap where you think the right angle is hiding.
tool_hidden_triangle_finder.invariant: The bent stem keeps its length; rhombus diagonals cross at right angles and halve each other; the altitude halves the base of the equilateral triangle.

source_metadata.design: new_design v2 (docs/25 playbook, sections 11 and 13): an enrichment introduction with no objective, where Baudhāyana's story video stops on the doubling question and a free-try tool follows; one topic per mathematical idea with 2 to 4 concepts, the first of T2 resuming from the student's tries, the last of each being a practice concept with the recap, this idea's practice questions and ONE minimal interactive tool; summary topic last. Every video is an interactive Manim script that pauses at each example and question until the student answers. Geometry rules from the Division 4 architecture: a guess first, manipulate before explaining, Van Hiele levels, non-prototypical figures, units in answers, region maps for pointing.
history: The Śulba-Sūtras are Baudhāyana's rules for constructing shapes of an exact area; doubling a square is the first question the chapter asks.
Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra (c. 800 BCE): Verse 1.9 doubling, Verse 1.10 three and five times, Verse 1.12 the theorem, Verse 1.13 the triples, Verse 2.1 the proof by rearrangement.
Pythagoras (c. 500 BCE) lived a couple of hundred years after Baudhāyana.
Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE) proved that √2 is not a fraction.
Bhāskarāchārya (Bhāskara II), Līlāvatī: the lotus problem.
Fermat (17th century) wrote the margin note; Andrew Wiles read about it at 10 in 1963 and proved it in 1994.
source_metadata.hierarchy: module > segment > topic (topic_objective) > concepts (one objective each, none on enrichment)

van_hiele.rule: Every concept carries van_hiele_required. A concept is served only when the student's demonstrated level is at least that value; on a level mismatch, drop a level and rebuild with a manipulable figure instead of re-explaining at the higher level.

levels.3: relates properties and follows a short argument

how_to_use.intro: Geometry here is learned by moving pieces. Squares are cut, slid, folded and counted before any rule is named, because the invariant (the area does not change when pieces move) is the whole argument. Every topic runs: guess, manipulate, notice, name, reason, apply.

points.text: Each topic and each tool opens with a committed prediction (tap an answer, type a guess). The misconception shows up in the prediction, where it can be fixed.
points.title: Predict before you touch

points.text: Cutting, sliding and folding come before the explanation. The static picture and the formula come after the student has seen that the area stays the same.
points.title: Manipulate, then explain

points.text: The chapter finds the area of a square before it knows the side: 2 before √2, c² before c. Squaring turns a length into an area; the square root turns it back.
points.title: Area first, length second

points.text: Before any calculation the student finds the right angle and the side opposite it. Figures are drawn tilted, thin and in every orientation, never only upright.
points.title: Right angle first

points.text: Lengths carry cm, m or units; areas carry square units. An answer without its unit is not done.
points.title: Units in every answer

points.text: The chapter opens with Baudhāyana's question. The story video stops on the question of doubling a square, and the student tries it freely on a grid of pegs before anything is explained. The explanation resumes at the start of the next topic, beginning from the student's own tries.
points.title: A story, then a free try

points.text: Every video explains its idea with moving figures, and at every example or question it stops. It resumes only when the student has answered (or after two tries and a hint), and then it shows the solution.
points.title: Videos that wait for an answer

points.text: The last concept of every topic recaps, works the practice questions for that idea, and then hands over ONE minimal interactive tool: one screen, at most three controls, three or four tasks. The tool applies the idea; it never replaces the teaching.
points.title: One small tool per topic

Every video is an interactive Manim script (user rule, 29 Sep 2026): scenes that explain, ask (the video pauses until the student answers), solve and recap, with manim_instructions and interaction_points; at most 5 questions per video. Tools reserve 2dtool_v3 and carry minimal specs.
source_metadata.chapter_idea: A square's area is not its side. Baudhāyana doubles, halves and combines squares by drawing them on diagonals and hypotenuses, and that leads to a² + b² = c² for every right triangle, to the strange length √2, to endless whole-number triples, and to Fermat's 350-year puzzle.

Try This icons (book): 2.3 'Can √2 be expressed as a fraction m/n', end Figure it Out 8 (ii), end Figure it Out 9.

End Figure it Out 2 figures, read at 260 dpi, in reading order: (a) legs 7 and 9; (b) legs 4 and 10; (c) leg 40, hypotenuse 41; (d) leg 10, hypotenuse √200; (e) legs 10 and √150; (f) leg 27, hypotenuse 45. (a) to (e) are drawn tilted; (c) has its right angle at the far-left corner, (d) at the top, (e) at the bottom with the hypotenuse on top; (f) is upright, its right angle at the bottom left (re-checked at 170 dpi, 29 Sep 2026).
End Figure it Out 8 grid: 5 by 5 dots.
The text layer of the PDF drops every √ and every superscript; all such values were read from the rendered pages.

misconceptions.fix: Double the side and count: 4 of the old squares fit inside.
misconceptions.text: Doubling the side of a square doubles its area (it makes 4 times the area).

misconceptions.fix: Fold the paper into four half-side squares: each is one quarter.
misconceptions.text: Halving the side of a square halves its area (it leaves one quarter).

misconceptions.fix: Count the congruent pieces before and after: the same pieces, the same area.
misconceptions.text: Cutting and moving pieces changes the area.

misconceptions.fix: Square the decimal: its last digit is never 0, so it is never exactly 2.0.
misconceptions.text: √2 is exactly 1.414, or ends where the calculator screen ends.

misconceptions.fix: Add the squares, not the sides: 6 + 8 = 14 but 6² + 8² = 100 = 10².
misconceptions.text: The hypotenuse is the sum of the legs, c = a + b.

misconceptions.fix: Find the right angle first; the hypotenuse is the side opposite it, whatever the orientation.
misconceptions.text: The hypotenuse is the bottom side, or the last side named.

misconceptions.fix: Given the hypotenuse, subtract: b² = c² − a².
misconceptions.text: Always add the squares, even when the hypotenuse is given.

misconceptions.fix: Only with a right angle: sides 5, 6, 7 give 25 + 36 = 61, not 49.
misconceptions.text: a² + b² = c² holds in every triangle.

misconceptions.fix: Rotate the figure: the right angle and the side opposite it do not change.
misconceptions.text: Only an upright right triangle with a horizontal base counts.

misconceptions.fix: A side is in cm; the square on it is in square cm.
misconceptions.text: Units are dropped, or cm and cm² are mixed.

misconceptions.fix: Multiply, do not add: (3, 4, 5) plus 1 is (4, 5, 6), and 16 + 25 = 41 is not 36.
misconceptions.text: Adding the same number to a triple gives another triple.

misconceptions.fix: There are infinitely many numbers; only a proof covers them all.
misconceptions.text: Checking many cases proves a statement about all numbers.

solution_notes.correct: Only in an isosceles RIGHT triangle, with c the hypotenuse; in a general isosceles triangle 2a² = c² is false.
solution_notes.printed_solution: In an isosceles triangle with sidelengths a, a, c, a² + a² = 2a² = c²

solution_notes.item: 2.5, the list of triples with numbers up to 20
solution_notes.correct: The full list also has (5, 12, 13) and (8, 15, 17): six triples. The book's word 'contains' is true, and it asks for the other primitive triples later.
Each equal side is √50, between 7.07 and 7.08; not a whole number.
Read as (√2)² = 2, the square of √2; not √(2²).
triangle congruence; Baudhāyana's instructions (kept verbatim in the textbook text).
